explain.say: A glider has no engine, so it is always sliding gently downhill through the air, trading height for speed. The trick to staying up is finding air that rises faster than the glider sinks.

faq.a: A thermal is a rising column of warm air, made when the sun heats a patch of ground like a field or a town. Glider pilots and soaring birds circle inside thermals to gain height.

Glide ratio is how far a glider travels forward for each metre of height it loses. Modern gliders manage 40 to 1 or better and the best about 60 to 1, while an airliner with its engines off is roughly 15 to 1.
asks: How far can a glider glide?

faq.q: How does a glider move forward without an engine?
faq.a: It points slightly downhill, so part of gravity pulls it forward, like a bike coasting down a gentle slope. The wings turn that slow descent into a long forward flight.

faq.q: How does a glider take off?
faq.a: Usually a powered plane tows it into the air on a rope, or a ground winch pulls it up like a kite. Once high enough, the pilot releases the rope.
asks: How do gliders get into the air?

faq.q: How long can a glider stay up?
faq.a: With good thermals or mountain waves, flights of many hours and hundreds of kilometres are common. The world distance record is over 3,000 kilometres.
asks: What is the glider distance record?

facts: The best competition gliders have glide ratios of around 60 to 1.
Soaring birds such as eagles and vultures use thermals the same way glider pilots do.

quiz.say: A glider pilot finds a thermal. What do they do to gain height?
quiz.show: In a thermal, the glider pilot…
quiz.why: Circling keeps the glider inside the rising column, so it is carried upward.

wrong.1: Diving trades height for speed, losing height quickly.
wrong.2: Leaving the thermal leaves the rising air behind.
